bib.title: Confidence Bounds for Least Squares Estimators (Bandit Algorithms, ch. 20)
bib.venue: book chapter (Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press)

question: Why does the LinUCB confidence set of the previous chapter hold when actions are chosen adaptively by a bandit algorithm?
contributions: Fixed-design confidence bound for ridge/OLS estimates via covering (Eq. 20.3)
Self-normalised martingale bound via the method of mixtures (Thms 20.4, 20.5), valid for all t simultaneously with adaptively chosen actions

results.claim: Fixed design, no regularisation: the confidence bound for a single direction x has width independent of d.
results.setup: Fixed design, lambda=0, independent 1-subgaussian noise, a fixed x

results.claim: Covering the unit sphere needs at most (3/eps)^d points.
results.setup: eps-cover of the unit sphere S^{d-1} in R^d
results.quote: Lemma 20.1. There exists a set Cε ⊂Rd with |Cε| ≤(3/ε)d

results.claim: Covering argument with eps = 1/2 gives a fixed-design confidence set of radius 2 sqrt(2(d log 6 + log(1/delta))).
results.setup: Fixed design, lambda=0, V_t deterministic; the argument fails for bandit-chosen actions

results.claim: Self-normalised bound (Thm 20.5): w.p. >= 1-delta, for all t, ||theta_hat_t - theta*||_{V_t(lambda)} < sqrt(lambda)||theta*||_2 + sqrt(2 log(1/delta) + log(det V_t(lambda)/lambda^d)).
results.setup: Conditionally 1-subgaussian noise, lambda>0, adaptive actions, infinite horizon
results.quote: Furthermore, if ∥θ∗∥2 ≤m2, then P (exists t ∈N+ : θ∗/∈Ct) ≤δ with
results.note: Proof via the method of mixtures with Gaussian prior h=N(0, (lambda I)^-1); maximal inequality for a supermartingale

results.claim: With lambda=1 and ||A_t||<=L the radius is m2 + sqrt(2 log(1/delta) + d log(1 + nL^2/d)), matching the fixed-design rate up to a sqrt(log n) factor; the sqrt(d) factor cannot be avoided.
results.quote: factor, is the same as what we got in the ﬁxed design case (cf. Eq. (20.3)),

results.claim: Going through a confidence set for the whole parameter adds a sqrt(d) factor to the width at a fixed input x, versus the d-free width of Eq. 20.2; a sequential design can force Omega(d).
results.quote: In the exercise, you will show that there

results.claim: Method of mixtures improves a lot over covering arguments in practice.
results.quote: In practice, the improvement provided by the method of mixtures relative to the covering arguments is quite large.

limits: Fixed-design analysis assumes lambda=0, independence and deterministic V_t, none valid for bandits.
Open question: confidence bounds at a fixed x under sequential design that adapt to the amount of dependence (Note 3).
Assumes conditionally 1-subgaussian noise and knowledge of a bound on ||theta*||.
practices: When confidence intervals are used inside an algorithm, prefer the log-determinant form log(det V_t(lambda)/lambda^d) to the looser trace/(1+nL^2/(lambda d))^d form (Note 1, p.261).
For a high-probability bound on the mean at one fixed input x, do not go through a confidence set for the whole parameter vector (Note 3, p.261).
Use lambda=1 to get the concrete confidence set C_t with radius m2 + sqrt(2 log(1/delta) + d log(1+nL^2/d)) (Note 2, p.261).

terms.definition: theta_hat_t = V_t(lambda)^-1 sum X_s A_s with V_t(lambda)=lambda I + sum A_s A_s^T
Bounds like those given in Theorem 20.5 are called self-normalised bounds [de la Peña et al., 2008].
Replace max_x M_t(x) by the integral of M_t(x) against a probability measure h, which stays a non-negative supermartingale (Lemma 20.3).

lineage.note: Justifies the confidence set used in the regret bound of the previous chapter
Exercise 20.10 result with constant c about 3.43

figures.caption: The plots depict Laplace's approximation with f(x) = cos(x) exp(−x2/20), which is maximised at x0 = 0 and has q = −f ′′(x0) = 11/10. The solid line is a plot of exp(sf(x))/exp(sf(x0)), and the dotted line is exp(−sq(x −x0)2).
figures.why: Shows exp(s f) approaching a Gaussian around its max as s goes 1 to 3; motivates replacing max with an integral. Theory-only, low value for a practitioner note.
